label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
**About the house in Glenmore**

I have news, and I'm putting it here so that everybody gets it at the same time and in the same words, whether you're reading in Boston or Perth or Leeds or a few miles down the road from me. Úna set this blog up years ago so the family could keep up with one another, and I can't think of a better use for it than this.

I have agreed a sale on the house in Glenmore. It was agreed on the 3rd of November and it closes on Friday the 15th of January. From that day the house will belong to a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. I'll tell you about them further down.

Some of you know already, and some of you who know did not hear it from me. That is my own fault and nobody else's. I hadn't told everyone properly before the news started to travel, and it travelled the way news does in this family, in bits, on the phone, from one cousin to the next. Nobody who passed it on did anything wrong. They took it that I'd already told the people who most needed telling, and I hadn't.

So before I give any reasons, I am sorry for how you found out. If you heard from somebody else that the Mulkerrin place was being sold, you were entitled to hear it from me. I knew that, and I left it too long anyway. I spent my working life telling small children to own up before they were found out, and I didn't manage it myself this time.

I am not sorry for the decision. I'd rather say so plainly than leave anyone thinking that a few hard phone calls might change it. They won't. What I can do is tell you everything that went into it, including one thing I've kept to myself for most of a year, and you can make of it what you will.

First the house itself, for the younger ones who may not have the history. Tom's grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin, built it in 1931, outside Oughterard, and Tom grew up in it. It has been in Tom's family for ninety-five years. I know well what I'm selling, and I've had long enough to think about it.

Tom died in March 2024. Since then I have driven out to Glenmore every fortnight, forty minutes there and forty minutes back, to air the house and check the pipes. A house that nobody lives in has to be minded or it goes against you, and I have been the one minding it. I did it through two winters and I've started on a third.

In September I had Ó Flaithearta's out to survey the roof. The slates need doing and so does the back chimney, and the quote came to €38,000. That figure doesn't include the damp in the back bedroom, which is a job of its own. On top of that, the septic tank needs replacing. That would have to be done to sell the house to anybody at all, so there was no road open to me that avoided it.

I'm giving you the figures because I'd want them if I were in your place. The house is asking for the guts of forty thousand euro before anyone so much as looks at the damp. When all that was done it would still be an empty house, forty minutes from the woman who has to keep it.

Now the thing I haven't told anyone.

Last February I was out there on one of my visits and I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I was able to get up. I was on my own, as I always am out there. I got myself up in the end and I told nobody, not that day and not since. This is the first any of you are hearing of it.

I should have told you. It's a large part of why I've done what I've done, and you couldn't be expected to understand the decision with that piece missing. The truth is that I have been afraid of being alone at that house ever since. I've kept going out every fortnight, because the pipes don't care whether I'm afraid or not, but I haven't had one easy visit since that day. I'm seventy-one. I think about that step every time I put my foot on it, and I think about how long twenty minutes is when you're lying on cold ground wondering if you'll be able to stand.

Put those things together and you have my reasons. I cannot go on maintaining the house. I can't keep up with what it needs, and I can't go on being out there by myself. I turned it over every way I could, and it came out the same each time.

The people buying it are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so he's no stranger to that country, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house. It will be their home all the year round and it will not be a holiday let. They've told me so and I believe them.

The price is a fair one. It is also less than I was offered in the summer by the Dublin crowd, and I want you to know that I took the lower offer on purpose. Nobody talked me into it and I didn't misread the figures.

Tom always said that house should have children in it and not be a museum. He said it more than once and he meant it. Since he died it has been turning into the very thing he didn't want, with me as the caretaker, calling every fortnight to open the windows and close them again. When a young family came along wanting to rear their children in it, I wasn't going to turn them away for the sake of the difference. Some of you may think I've been soft about money. You may be right, and I'd do the same again tomorrow.

Not everything is going with the house. This is what's being kept:

- The dresser, which is going to Úna's.
- Pádraig's fiddle.
- The photographs.
- The Sacred Heart lamp.
- The sign from the gate.

If you asked me what the house is, once you take away the slates and the damp, I think I'd point to those things before I'd point to any wall.

The Joyces have also said that the family can come out and walk the land any time. I hope you'll take them at their word. I intend to.

I don't want anyone to think the place means less to me than it does to you. Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind that house in 1979. It was raining, and the cattle stood and watched the whole thing. I can't go round the back of the house without seeing it.

Our children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Declan could not be got out of the water. He'd refuse to come in until his lips were blue. I can see that too, any time I like, and I don't need to be standing on the shore to do it.

It has taken me the best part of two years to learn that I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I didn't believe it at the start. For a long time after he died, the house and Tom were the one thing to me, and minding it felt like minding him. I think that's why I kept driving out when sense would have told me to stop.

Somewhere along all those drives out and back, the two came apart. Tom isn't in the slates or the chimney. He is in the haggard in 1979 whether I own the haggard or not, and nobody can sell that or buy it. I don't expect all of you to have arrived at the same place. I'm only telling you where I've got to and how long it took me.

Declan, I know you read these, so this part is for you, and I don't mind who else reads it.

You heard about the sale from Gráinne, on WhatsApp, and you should have heard it from me. Gráinne did nothing wrong. You rang me at two in the morning your time and you told me I was selling Dad. I said things back to you that I shouldn't have said, and I wish I could have them back.

I am not angry with you. I wasn't angry the next morning and I'm not now. You were upset because you love that house and you loved your father, and I'd have thought less of you if you'd taken it calmly.

I regret that I didn't consult you. You are his son and you grew up in and out of that lake. You should have been asked what you thought before it was settled, and not told after, and by somebody else at that. That is on me.

But I'm not willing to wait until your visit in the summer, and I won't pretend to be considering it. The sale closes in January. Waiting would mean another winter of that drive and that step, with the roof getting no better. I can't do it, and now you know why.

I am not selling your father. I couldn't if I tried. I'm selling a house he loved to people who will fill it with children, which is what he said he wanted for it.

The door is open. Ring me at any hour you like, two in the morning included, and say whatever you need to say. I'll do better at listening than I did the last time.

Now, the day out. Before the house is cleared, I'd like us to have one day in it together. It will be on Sunday the 13th of December, at the house, for anyone who can come. There'll be soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, because the ground will be what it always is in December. I want people to be able to go down to the lake and round to the haggard and anywhere else they'd like to stand for a minute.

The house will still have its things in it. You can sit in the kitchen, look at the photographs where they've always hung and hear the fiddle if anyone is able to get a tune out of it. Let me know if you're coming so I know how much soup to make.

I know that for a good many of you a Sunday in December in Connemara is out of the question. Nobody will think the less of anyone who can't be there, and the Joyces' offer about the land stands for whenever you're home.

So, once more, so that nobody is depending on anyone else for it: the sale was agreed on the 3rd of November, the family day is Sunday the 13th of December, and the house passes to the Joyces on Friday the 15th of January.

That is all of it, and I've kept nothing back this time. If you hear anything about the house that isn't written here, ring me and ask, and I'll tell you.

---

A few things to check before you post it:

- **Time and name:** I didn't put a time on the 13th of December or sign it, since I didn't have either.
- **Úna and Declan:** I left out how Úna is related and where Declan lives, because your notes didn't say.
- **Small additions of mine:** These are the line about telling children to own up, hearing the fiddle on the day, and asking people to say if they're coming. Cut any that aren't true to you.
- **Length:** It comes to roughly 2,000 words, the short end of what you asked for. I didn't want to pad it with memories I'd have had to make up.
